paragraphs: “What are you saying? I’m lost again,” Miüsov broke in. “Another sort of dream. Something shapeless, even impossible to grasp. What is this excommunication? What kind of exclusion? I suspect you’re just amusing yourself, Ivan Fyodorovitch.”

“Yes, but you know, in reality it is so even now,” said the elder suddenly, and all turned to him at once. “Without the Church of Christ, nothing would hold the criminal back from doing evil, and there would be no real punishment for it afterward. I mean no punishment but the mechanical kind spoken of just now, which in most cases only embitters the heart. I mean not the real punishment, the only effective one, the only one that deters and softens, which lies in the conscience’s own recognition of sin.”
“How is that, may I ask?” Miüsov asked, with lively curiosity.

“Why,” began the elder, “all these sentences of exile with hard labor, and in the past with flogging too, reform no one. What is more, they hardly deter a single criminal, and crimes do not grow fewer but keep on increasing. You must admit that. So society is not made safe. The harmful member is cut off mechanically and sent far away, out of sight. But another criminal at once comes to take his place, and often two. If anything protects society, even in our time, and does regenerate and transform the criminal, it is only the law of Christ speaking in his conscience. Only when he sees his wrongdoing as a son of a Christian society—that is, of the Church—does he see his sin against society—that is, against the Church. So the criminal of today can recognize that he has sinned only against the Church, not against the State. If society, as a Church, held jurisdiction, it would know when to call a man back from exclusion and join him to itself again. But the Church has no real jurisdiction, only the power of moral condemnation, and so she of her own accord refrains from punishing the criminal in practice. She does not excommunicate him. She simply goes on exhorting him as a mother would. More than that, the Church tries to keep up full Christian fellowship with him. She lets him attend church services and receive the holy sacrament, she gives him alms, and she treats him more as a captive than as a convict. And what would become of the criminal, O Lord, if even Christian society—that is, the Church—rejected him, as the civil law rejects him and cuts him off? What would become of him if the Church punished him with excommunication as the direct consequence of the secular law? There could be no more terrible despair, at least for a Russian criminal, for Russian criminals still have faith. Yet who knows? Perhaps something fearful would happen then. Perhaps the criminal’s despairing heart would lose its faith, and then what would become of him? But the Church, like a tender, loving mother, keeps back from active punishment herself, because the sinner is already punished too severely by the civil law, and someone at least must have pity on him. Above all, the Church keeps back because her judgment alone holds the truth. So it cannot be joined, in practice or in morals, to any other judgment, even as a temporary compromise. She can make no bargain over that. The foreign criminal, they say, rarely repents, since the very doctrines of today persuade him that his crime is no crime, only a reaction against an unjustly oppressive force. Society cuts him off completely, by a force that overpowers him mechanically. (So at least they say of themselves in Europe.) It accompanies this exclusion with hatred, forgetfulness, and the deepest indifference to the final fate of the erring brother. So it all happens without the compassionate intervention of the Church, for in many places there are no churches at all. Churchmen and splendid church buildings remain, but the churches themselves long ago strove to pass from Church into State and disappear into it entirely. So it seems, at least, in Lutheran countries. As for Rome, it was proclaimed a State instead of a Church a thousand years ago. And so the criminal no longer feels himself a member of the Church, and sinks into despair. If he returns to society, he often does so with such hatred that society itself instinctively cuts him off. You can judge for yourself how it must end. In many cases it might seem to be the same with us. But the difference is that, besides the established law courts, we have the Church too, which always keeps up its bond with the criminal as a dear and still precious son. And there is something more. The judgment of the Church is still preserved, though only in thought. It no longer exists in practice, but it lives on as a dream for the future, and the criminal, no doubt, recognizes it instinctively in his soul. What was said here just now is also true: if the jurisdiction of the Church were brought into practice in its full force—if the whole of society were changed into the Church—then the Church’s judgment would influence the reformation of the criminal as it never does now. Possibly, too, crimes themselves would become incredibly fewer. And there can be no doubt that the Church would regard the criminal, and the crime of the future, quite differently in many cases. She would succeed in restoring the excluded, in restraining those who plan evil, and in raising up the fallen. It is true,” said Father Zossima, with a smile, “Christian society is not ready now and rests only on some seven righteous men. But since they are never lacking, it will stand unshaken, awaiting its complete transformation from a society almost heathen in character into a single, universal and all-powerful Church. So be it, so be it! Even if it comes at the end of the ages, for it is ordained to come to pass! And there is no need to be troubled about times and seasons, for the secret of the times and seasons lies in the wisdom of God, in His foresight and His love. What seems still far off by human reckoning may, by Divine ordinance, be close at hand, on the eve of its appearing. And so be it, so be it!”
“So be it, so be it!” Father Païssy repeated sternly and reverently.
“Strange, extremely strange!” Miüsov declared, not so much with heat as with suppressed indignation.
“What strikes you as so strange?” Father Iosif asked cautiously.

“Why, it’s out of all bounds!” cried Miüsov, suddenly bursting out. “The State is abolished and the Church is raised to the rank of the State. It’s not just Ultramontanism, it’s arch-Ultramontanism! Pope Gregory the Seventh never dreamed of such a thing!”

“You have got it completely wrong,” said Father Païssy sternly. “Understand this: the Church is not to be turned into the State. That is Rome and its dream. That is the devil’s third temptation. It is the other way around. The State is turned into the Church. It will rise and become a Church over the whole world. That is the exact opposite of Ultramontanism and Rome, and of your reading of it. It is simply the glorious destiny ordained for the Orthodox Church. This star will rise in the east!”

Miüsov said nothing, and the silence was pointed. Everything about him spoke of extraordinary personal dignity. A superior, patronizing smile played on his lips. Alyosha watched it all, his heart pounding. The whole conversation had shaken him deeply. In passing, he glanced at Rakitin, who stood rooted to his spot by the door, listening and watching closely, though his eyes were lowered. Alyosha guessed from the color in his cheeks that Rakitin was probably just as excited, and he knew what excited him.

“Allow me to tell you a little anecdote, gentlemen,” Miüsov said impressively, with a peculiarly majestic air. “Some years ago, soon after the _coup d’état_ of December, I happened to be calling in Paris on an extremely influential figure in the Government, and at his house I met a very interesting man. He was not exactly a detective, but a sort of superintendent over a whole regiment of political detectives—a rather powerful position in its own way. Curiosity prompted me to seize the chance to talk with him. He had not come as a visitor but as a subordinate bringing a special report, and he saw the reception his chief gave me. So he condescended to speak with some openness—to a certain extent only, of course. He was more courteous than open, as Frenchmen know how to be courteous, especially to a foreigner. But I understood him perfectly. The subject was the socialist revolutionaries, who were being persecuted at that time. I will quote only one most curious remark this man let drop. ‘We are not particularly afraid,’ he said, ‘of all these socialists, anarchists, infidels and revolutionists. We keep watch on them and know all their doings. But there are a few peculiar men among them who believe in God and are Christians, yet are socialists all the same. Those are the people we fear most. They are dreadful people! The socialist who is a Christian is more to be dreaded than a socialist who is an atheist.’ The words struck me at the time, and now they have suddenly come back to me here, gentlemen.”
“You apply them to us, and take us for socialists?” Father Païssy asked bluntly, without beating about the bush.

But before Pyotr Alexandrovitch could think what to answer, the door opened and the long-awaited guest, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, came in. They had in fact given up expecting him, and his sudden appearance caused a moment of surprise.
